summary: Describes private SIP header fields used by 3GPP for purposes such as charging and information about networks a call passes through, along with their limited applicability. It obsoletes RFC 3455.

plainLanguage.summary: Phone networks built on SIP needed to pass extra facts between their own servers, such as which number a call was meant for, which network a travelling phone is using, and how to bill for a call that spans networks. This memo defines six private message fields for those jobs and stresses that they only make sense inside trusted private networks, not on the open Internet.

subtitle: The private SIP header fields 3GPP mobile networks use to carry identity, network and charging information.

tldr.problem: The 3GPP IP Multimedia Subsystem needs SIP to carry information that ordinary SIP does not provide, such as which of a user's addresses a call was sent to, which visited network is serving a roaming user, and the identifiers needed to correlate charging records.
tldr.mechanism: It defines six private, or P-, header fields, each with a forceful applicability statement that limits its use to private networks where the proxies share trust relationships and the extension's assumptions hold.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 3455, and it was later updated by RFC 7913, RFC 7976 and RFC 9878.

today: RFC 7315 is an Informational RFC published in July 2014. It obsoletes RFC 3455 and has been updated by RFC 7913, RFC 7976 and RFC 9878. Its headers remain limited to private 3GPP networks.

sections.title: Why Private Headers Exist
sections.content:
The extensions in this document rest on assumptions about network topology, the link between SIP and the layers below it, and the availability of transitive trust. Those assumptions hold only in private networks and are not appropriate for the Internet environment. The mechanisms were designed to satisfy the 3GPP Release 5 requirements on SIP for which either no general-purpose solution was planned or no mature general solution existed.

The 3GPP uses SIP to set up and tear down multimedia sessions in its IP Multimedia Subsystem. This memo updates the private header descriptions to address additional requirements needed for 3GPP Release 11, and it obsoletes RFC 3455.
sections.plainLanguage: These fields are meant for phone operators' own private networks, where the servers already trust one another. They are not for use on the open Internet. The memo refreshes an older one and adds what newer phone networks need.

sections.title: Headers About Identity and Networks
sections.content:
Four of the six fields deal with identity and location. The P-Associated-URI field lets a registrar return, in the 200 (OK) response to a REGISTER request, the set of URIs associated with a registered address-of-record, so a user agent can see which other identities the provider has granted it. The P-Called-Party-ID field is inserted, typically in an INVITE request, and carries the Request-URI as it was before the proxy retargeted it to a contact address; it lets a user agent that registered several addresses know which one the call was sent to, for example to choose a different ring tone. It is especially useful when the To header cannot be trusted, for instance after a call was forwarded. This field is used entirely within the 3GPP system and does not appear outside a single operator.

The P-Visited-Network-ID field identifies the visited network serving a roaming user, so the home network can check a roaming agreement and authorize the registration; it reveals the user's location to the level of the visited network's coverage. The P-Access-Network-Info field relays details of the access technology, such as radio access technology and cell identity, so the home serving proxy can tailor services or provide location-based services; this information is potentially very sensitive. A proxy must not modify its value and must delete it before sending toward an untrusted administrative domain. These extensions assume transitive trust between the user agent and the serving proxy, supported by mechanisms such as IPsec, AKA or TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Four of the fields describe who is calling or being called and where they are. One lists the extra identities a provider has given a user; one records which identity a call was aimed at before it was rerouted; one names the network a travelling phone is visiting; and one passes technical details of the radio access, which can reveal roughly where the user is. The last one is treated as sensitive and must be removed before messages leave the trusted network.

sections.title: Headers About Charging
sections.content:
The remaining two fields support charging in a distributed network. The P-Charging-Function-Addresses field tells each proxy which charging entities should receive the charging records. The 3GPP defines two kinds: the Charging Collection Function for offline, postpaid charging, and the Event Charging Function for online, prepaid charging. More than one instance of each may exist for redundancy, and implementations should try the first address in the sequence and fall back to the next if it is unavailable. The header is used within a single private administrative domain and must be removed when a message leaves that domain.

The P-Charging-Vector field carries correlation information so that records generated by different entities for the same session can be tied together. It holds three kinds of information: the IMS Charging Identity (ICID), which is a globally unique value identifying a dialog or transaction; the address of the proxy that created the ICID; and the Inter Operator Identifier (IOI), which identifies the originating and terminating networks. Transit networks may be listed as they are traversed, and a void value may stand in for a network whose name the operator does not wish to reveal. The field is used within a private domain or between domains that share a trust relationship. Each of the two headers must appear at most once in a request or response.
sections.plainLanguage: The last two fields handle billing. One tells the servers where to send their billing records, with backups in case the first is down. The other gives a shared identifier so the records from different servers about the same call can be matched up, and names the networks involved.

sections.title: Security and Scope
sections.content:
The security discussion is given per field, and its theme is that these extensions only make sense where the right relationships exist. The P-Associated-URI field assumes the provider knows the whole set of identities a user may legitimately claim. The P-Called-Party-ID field assumes the proxy inserting it has reliable information about the user. The P-Visited-Network-ID field reveals the user's location to the coverage area of the visited network and relies on transitive trust in intermediate proxies. The P-Access-Network-Info field reveals potentially very sensitive information, so the user agent must know that the trust relationships needed to protect it exist, and a proxy sending to an untrusted entity must remove network-provided values. The two charging fields are confined to a private administrative domain, or to domains that trust each other, and must be removed before a message leaves.

Overall the RFC is explicit that these fields carry information that ordinary SIP would not, and that they are not for general Internet use. This document obsoletes RFC 3455 and updates the header descriptions for 3GPP Release 11.
sections.plainLanguage: Every one of these fields is safe only when the servers along the way already trust each other and when the user knows those relationships are in place. Some of the fields reveal location or identity, so they are stripped out before messages cross into a network that is not trusted.

items.title: P-Associated-URI
items.text: Lists the URIs linked to a registered address-of-record.

items.title: P-Called-Party-ID
items.text: Records the address a call was sent to before retargeting.

items.title: P-Visited-Network-ID
items.text: Names the visited network serving a roaming user.

items.title: P-Access-Network-Info
items.text: Carries access technology and cell information.

items.title: P-Charging-Function-Addresses
items.text: Points proxies at the charging entities.

items.title: P-Charging-Vector
items.text: Correlates charging records for one session.
